title: Long-term residence in pathogen-endemic environments is associated with distinct immune states
description: Long-term residence in pathogen-endemic environments may shape baseline immune homeostasis, yet its effects in clinically healthy adults remain unclear. We profiled peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) transcriptomes and plasma mediators in 60 Kenyan adults from regions with differing infectious exposure burdens. Individuals from higher-exposure areas exhibited widespread transcriptional changes, with 658 genes differentially expressed and enrichment of pathways related to B-cell activation, antigen presentation, immune regulation, and post-transcriptional mRNA processing. In contrast, inflammatory, chemotactic, and vascular gene programs were downregulated, indicating restrained inflammatory transcription despite adaptive immune activation. Plasma mediators were modestly elevated despite reduced inflammatory transcription in PBMCs, revealing partial dissociation between circulating analyte levels and cellular transcriptional profiles. Our findings suggest that long-term residence in pathogen-endemic environments is associated with distinct immune states characterised by adaptive activation and restrained inflammatory transcription, with potential implications for responses to secondary infections and vaccination.
